notes.h: What variation is, and where it comes from
notes.b: No two members of a species are exactly alike. These differences are called variation, and they have two very different origins: the genes an organism inherits and the conditions it lives in.
points: Variation is the differences between individuals of the same species, such as in height, eye colour, blood group or resistance to a disease.
Genetic (inherited) variation is caused by differences in alleles (the different versions of a gene) and genes, so it can be passed to offspring in the DNA.

Environmental (acquired) variation is caused by the conditions an organism lives in, e.g. a scar, a suntan, muscles built by exercise, or a plant's size in poor soil. It is not passed on through the DNA, so a parent's exercised muscles do not appear in its children.
Most characteristics depend on both causes: phenotype (the observable trait) = genotype (the alleles an organism carries) + environment. For example, height is set by genes but also depends on diet.
Only genetic variation matters for evolution, because only it can be inherited and acted on by natural selection (the survival and reproduction of the best-suited individuals).
notes.tip: A common question asks for two causes of variation within a species: give genetic differences (alleles) and the environment, with an example of each. Never say acquired characteristics such as exercised muscles are inherited.

notes.b: Traits vary in two patterns. Some sort individuals into a few clear groups, while others spread them along a smooth range. The pattern tells you how many genes are involved and how much the environment matters.
points: Discontinuous variation: individuals fall into a few distinct groups with no in-between forms, e.g. the human ABO blood group, round or wrinkled pea seeds, or albinism (lack of pigment).

Discontinuous traits are usually controlled by one or a few genes, with little effect from the environment, so a person cannot change their blood group by diet or lifestyle. The data are shown in a bar chart, because each group is a separate category.
Continuous variation: individuals show a smooth range between two extremes, e.g. human height, mass, skin colour or leaf length.

Continuous traits are usually controlled by many genes together with the environment, so there are many small steps between the extremes. Most individuals are near the middle, giving a bell-shaped (normal) distribution shown in a histogram.

Diagram: a bar chart of the four ABO blood groups (discontinuous) beside a bell-shaped histogram of height in a class (continuous). Labels: blood group or height class on the x-axis; number of people on the y-axis.
notes.tip: Be ready to say which type a given trait is and why: distinct groups, one or few genes and a bar chart mean discontinuous; a smooth range, many genes plus environment and a histogram mean continuous.

notes.b: Sexual reproduction does not make new genes. It reshuffles the alleles already in the population, and it does so so thoroughly that each offspring is a new combination. Asexual reproduction, with no shuffling, shows what is lost without it.
points: Sexual reproduction does not create new alleles. It produces new combinations of existing alleles in every generation, so every offspring (except identical twins) is genetically unique.

Independent assortment: which chromosome of each homologous pair (the two matching chromosomes, one from each parent) enters a gamete (sex cell) is random and independent of the other pairs. One person can therefore make 2²³, about 8.4 million, different combinations of chromosomes in their gametes.

Random fertilisation: any one of the father's millions of sperm types can fertilise any one of the mother's egg types. Two parents can therefore produce about 8.4 million × 8.4 million, about 70 trillion (7 × 10¹³), different combinations of chromosomes, before other sources of variation are counted.
Two parents: each offspring combines alleles from two different individuals, so alleles that arose in different family lines come together. The choice of mate also varies, which adds further variety.

Asexual reproduction has one parent and no gametes. Cells divide by mitosis (bacteria divide by binary fission), so offspring are genetically identical clones, e.g. bacteria, potato tubers and strawberry runners. Their only source of genetic variation is mutation.
A population of clones may all be destroyed by the same disease or change in the environment, because none has a different allele that could resist it.

Example of the risk: the potatoes grown in Ireland before the Great Famine were mostly a single variety, the Lumper, propagated from tubers, so the plants were almost genetically identical. When potato blight, caused by Phytophthora infestans, arrived in 1845, none was resistant and the crop failed across the country.

Diagram: two homologous pairs (one long, one short, coloured to show the chromosome from the mother and from the father) in a cell, the two possible ways they can line up before separating, and the four resulting kinds of gamete. Labels: homologous pair, gamete, maternal chromosome, paternal chromosome.
notes.tip: To explain why sexual reproduction gives variation but asexual does not, name independent assortment, random fertilisation and two parents, and say the asexual offspring are identical clones. Do not say sexual reproduction creates new alleles; only mutation does.

notes.h: Mutation: the source of new alleles
notes.b: Sexual reproduction can only shuffle alleles that already exist. Mutation is the only source of new alleles, so it is the original source of all genetic variation.
points: A mutation is a change in the DNA: in the base sequence of a gene (the order of its chemical letters), or in the structure or number of chromosomes.
Mutations happen spontaneously, mainly as rare copying errors when DNA is replicated (copied before a cell divides).
Mutagens, such as ionising radiation (X-rays, gamma rays), ultraviolet light and certain chemicals, e.g. some in tobacco smoke, increase the rate of mutation.
Mutations are random: mutagens change the rate but not the direction. The environment does not cause a mutation that helps the organism adapt, and a need for a change does not make it happen.
Each gene mutates rarely, but there are many genes and many individuals, so new mutations arise in every generation.

Organisms that reproduce very fast, such as bacteria, accumulate mutations quickly because they pass through so many generations. Antibiotic resistance in bacteria is an example: a mutation that lets a bacterium survive an antibiotic is quickly passed on to its many descendants.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to define mutation and name two mutagens. Say a mutagen raises the rate of mutation; it does not make useful mutations happen on demand.

notes.b: Mutations are grouped by the size of the change. A gene mutation alters the letters of one gene, while a chromosome mutation changes a whole stretch of a chromosome, or the number of chromosomes.
points: Gene (point) mutation: a change in the base sequence of one gene, e.g. one base replaced by another, or a base added or lost. It creates a new allele of that gene.
Example of a gene mutation: sickle-cell anaemia is caused by a change of a single base in a gene for haemoglobin (the oxygen-carrying protein in red blood cells).

Chromosome mutation: a change in the structure of a chromosome, such as a section lost (deletion), copied (duplication), turned around (inversion) or moved to another chromosome (translocation). It affects many genes at once, because a chromosome carries many genes.

Changes in chromosome number also cause variation. Down syndrome is caused by an extra copy of chromosome 21 (47 chromosomes in total instead of 46). It is a change in number, not one of the four structural changes above.
In plants, whole extra sets of chromosomes (polyploidy) are common; bread wheat has six sets.
notes.tip: To distinguish gene and chromosome mutations, give an example of each: sickle-cell anaemia (a single-base change) for a gene mutation, and a lost, copied, inverted or moved section, or Down syndrome's extra chromosome 21, for chromosome changes.

notes.h: Effects of mutations, with lactase persistence
notes.b: A mutation is a random change, so it has no built-in tendency to help or harm. Its effect depends on what the change does and on the environment the organism lives in.
points: Most mutations are neutral (no effect, e.g. in non-coding DNA, or a change that gives the same amino acid) or harmful; a few are beneficial in a particular environment. So it is false to say a mutation always has a negative effect.
Chromosome mutations are usually harmful in animals, but polyploidy is often tolerated in plants, and many crop plants are polyploid.

Beneficial example, lactase persistence: most mammals stop making lactase, the enzyme that digests milk sugar, after weaning (when they stop drinking milk). A mutation in the DNA controlling the lactase gene keeps it switched on in adults.
The lactase mutation became common in populations with a long history of dairy farming, such as northern Europe including Ireland, because adults who could digest milk had an advantage.
notes.tip: If asked whether a mutation always has a negative impact, the answer is false: say most are neutral or harmful but a few are beneficial, and use lactase persistence as your example.

notes.b: A mutation only matters for the next generation if it reaches the gametes. The cell in which it happens decides whether it is inherited.
points: Only mutations in cells that make gametes (or in a gamete) are inherited, because only gametes join to form the next generation.
A mutation in a body cell (a somatic mutation), e.g. a skin cell damaged by ultraviolet light, affects only the cells descended from it and may cause cancer, but is not passed to offspring.
notes.tip: If asked why a mutation in a skin cell is not passed to offspring, say it is in a body cell, not a gamete, so it affects only that cell's descendants.

notes.b: Both processes produce genetic variation, but in different ways. Set side by side, they show why natural selection needs both.
points: What it does: sexual reproduction shuffles existing alleles into new combinations; mutation creates new alleles or new chromosome arrangements.
How often: sexual reproduction happens in every generation, in every offspring; mutation happens rarely and at random.

Effect on the individual: sexual reproduction makes every offspring different, but each allele in the new combination was already present and working in a parent. Most mutations are neutral or harmful, and a few are beneficial.
Organisms: sexual reproduction occurs only in sexually reproducing organisms; mutation occurs in all organisms, including those that reproduce asexually.
Together, mutation supplies new alleles and sexual reproduction spreads them into new combinations, giving the variation on which natural selection acts.
notes.tip: For compare questions, pair each point: shuffles existing alleles versus creates new ones, every generation versus rarely and at random, only sexual organisms versus all organisms.

keyTerms.definition: The differences between individuals of the same species.
Variation caused by differences in alleles and genes, which can be passed to offspring.
Variation caused by the conditions an organism lives in, which is not inherited.
Variation where individuals fall into a few distinct groups with no intermediate forms.
Variation where individuals show a smooth range between two extremes, usually controlled by many genes and the environment.
The random, independent sorting of each homologous pair of chromosomes into gametes, which creates variation.
A genetically identical offspring produced without fertilisation, e.g. by mitosis or binary fission.
A change in the base sequence of a gene or in the structure or number of chromosomes.
An agent, such as ionising radiation, ultraviolet light or certain chemicals, that increases the rate of mutation.
A mutation in a body cell, which affects only that cell's descendants and is not passed to offspring.

questions.prompt: Give two ways in which sexual reproduction produces variation, and explain why offspring produced asexually show little variation.
questions.model: Two ways: first, independent assortment of homologous chromosomes in meiosis, so each gamete receives a random mix of maternal and paternal chromosomes (about 8.4 million combinations per person); second, random fertilisation, since any sperm can fuse with any egg, giving about 70 trillion combinations from two parents. Asexual reproduction produces offspring by mitosis (or binary fission) with one parent and no gametes, so the offspring are clones that are genetically identical to the parent. There is no reshuffling of alleles, so the only new variation comes from rare mutation.

questions.prompt: Define mutation. Distinguish between a gene mutation and a chromosome mutation, giving one example of each.
questions.model: A mutation is a change in the DNA: in the base sequence of a gene, or in the structure or number of chromosomes. A gene mutation changes the base sequence of one gene, e.g. one base is replaced by another, creating a new allele; sickle-cell anaemia is caused by a change of a single base in a gene for haemoglobin. A chromosome mutation affects many genes at once, either by changing the structure of a chromosome (a section is lost by deletion, copied by duplication, turned around by inversion or moved to another chromosome by translocation) or by changing the number of chromosomes; Down syndrome, with an extra copy of chromosome 21 and 47 chromosomes in total, is an example of a change in number.

questions.prompt: Explain how mutation and sexual reproduction together provide the variation needed for evolution.
questions.model: Mutation is the only source of new alleles, so it is the original source of all genetic variation; it is random, rare, and occurs in gametes or in cells that make gametes, because only mutations in gametes are inherited. Most mutations are neutral or harmful, but a few are beneficial in a particular environment, as with the lactase mutation that allows adults to digest milk in populations with a history of dairy farming. Sexual reproduction then shuffles the existing alleles into new combinations: independent assortment in meiosis and random fertilisation mean that every offspring is genetically unique. The result is a population with a range of inherited differences, and only inherited variation can be acted on by natural selection, which is how evolution occurs.
